why.say: Quick game: True or False, hands up for true. One, an adjuster's deadline can bend if you ask nicely. Two, a court's deadline can bend if you ask nicely. {name}, you put your hand up for number two. Bold. Here's the truth: our 07/20/2026 Time-Limited Demand to Keystone lapsed unaccepted on 08/21/2026, and the 48-Hour Mandate got no answer. So Atty. Thorne made the call, and on 09/24/2026 John Doe's file became Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417. From that day, a judge sets the pace, not an adjuster. That's why we keep a Pleadings Log, which is just our running list of everything filed and served, and a Discovery Calendar, which is every date the other side owes us something or we owe them. And I'll warn you now: there's one kind of paper in this lesson that, if you ignore it, answers itself, against us. I'll show you which.
why.ask: {name}, now that we're in suit, who decides the very next legal step, and who makes sure it happens on time?

theory.say: In plain words, a lawsuit is a strict, step-by-step process the court runs, and if we miss a deadline or misfile something, the court can throw the case out. Your job changes by phase. In pleadings, which is the opening paperwork, you track service and set up the files. In discovery, which is when both sides have to show their cards, you gather data and prepare the client. In trial prep you line up schedules and pull the final medical records. Now, three discovery tools. Interrogatories are written questions answered under oath. Requests for production demand documents. And requests for admission, RFAs, demand that we admit or deny a statement. Every filing creates a docket entry, a line on the court's record, and its clock runs whether or not the email ever reached you. The lazy Case Manager says, “I never got it.” The court says, “Not my problem.”
theory.ask: {name}, of those three tools, which one do you think is the most dangerous to ignore, and why?

frame.say: Here's the whole lawsuit in three phases. Guess first, {name}: which phase eats most of a Case Manager's time? Hold it. Phase one is pleadings. The Complaint is filed, the defendant is served, and the Answer comes back, and you're tracking service and setting up the files. Phase two is discovery: interrogatories, requests for production, depositions, which are recorded interviews under oath. You calendar every response, gather the data and meet with the client. Phase three is trial prep: expert reports, motions, and then trial or settlement, and you coordinate schedules and update the final medicals. And the answer is discovery, almost every time. A Case Manager I trained called it “the season where every envelope has a stopwatch in it.” Know which phase you're in, and you know what your desk should look like this week. Because e-filing portals, by the way, always seem to crash at 11:59 p.m. on the last day, and only on the last day.
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file, which phase is he in right now, and how can you tell from the file?

rules.say: First rule: litigation isn't a longer negotiation. From the 09/24/2026 filing, the court sets the pace. Before Atty. Thorne signs the Complaint, you check the filing date against the SOL, the deadline to sue, and confirm the defendant's exact legal name. Service is the proof the defendant knew he was sued, so log every attempt. Still unserved at day 14, that was 10/08/2026, you escalate for Skip-Trace authority. A Skip-Trace is a paid professional search for someone's current address, so Atty. Thorne approves it first. Smith was served 10/14/2026. Now the paper I warned you about: the RFAs. Leave one unanswered past its deadline and it may be deemed admitted, meaning the court treats it as true. That's the paper that answers itself. When discovery lands, calendar it that day and book a Discovery Intake Meeting. The lazy move is mailing John Doe all 70 requests and saying “fill these out.” The high-value move is sitting down with him, one request at a time. You track and draft; Atty. Thorne decides and signs, and you never tell John Doe how to answer.
rules.ask: {name}, an RFA lands on your desk at 4:55 on a Friday. What do you do before you go home?

model.say: This master timeline has a trick hidden in it, and {name}, I want you to find it. It runs from 09/24/2026 to 01/13/2027, and each numbered badge is a trigger: the Complaint filed, Smith served on 10/14, the Answer on 11/12, discovery mailed 12/01, the Scheduling Order on 12/10, and our own set e-served 12/14. From every trigger, a line drops to its due date. Here's the trick: the 12/01 line is drawn in three steps. Plus 30 days, plus 3 days because it came by mail, and then Sunday rolls to Monday, landing on 01/04/2027. Miss any one of those steps and you're a day early or, worse, a day late. On the right is the warning I want burned in: 15 RFAs, unanswered means deemed admitted. Along the bottom sit the five numbered litigation sub-folders. Every date on our calendar is a calculation anyone can re-check, and that's what makes the defense take us seriously.
model.ask: {name}, if I hid the due dates, could you rebuild each one from its trigger alone, starting with 12/01?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. Atty. Thorne authorizes suit. Before he signs, you confirm Robert Smith's exact legal name from an independent record, like the Declaration Page or DMV records, not the Police Report alone. I once saw a complaint name the defendant's middle name as his last name, because somebody copied it off a crash report in a hurry. It took weeks to fix. Ours is filed 09/24/2026, well inside our 02/04/2028 internal hard date, and logged in the Pleadings Log, with the stamped complaint in 01_PLEADINGS the same day. A service attempt fails? Log it, and at day 14, 10/08/2026, escalate to Atty. Thorne with the attempt log and run the Skip-Trace on his approval. When the RFAs land, you calendar each response with the math written in and alert him within the hour, time-stamped. Why so strict? Because one deemed admission can hand the defense the very fact our whole case depends on.
job.ask: {name}, why does the Police Report alone not count as proof of Robert Smith's legal name?

dodont.say: Game time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues, one at a time, about something a Case Manager did on this file. Call it the moment you know: Do or Don't. Then name the rule behind it. Points go to whoever explains why, not whoever shouts first. {name}, you're on scorekeeping. {name}, you get the first buzz. The rules you need: the math written into every calendar entry, the baseline questions in every interrogatory set, recording John Doe's own words, the SOL, and counting from a trigger date. While you play, remember the difference. The bare-minimum Case Manager puts a date on the calendar. The high-value one puts the date and the arithmetic, so anybody can check it at midnight. Now your mystery: on this timeline, one response is due on a date that looks wrong but is actually right. {name}, find it and prove it before the next lesson.
dodont.ask: {name}, ready for the first clue? Who's brave enough to call it after just one?

why.say: Would you rather: an adjuster's letter with ten deadlines, or one page from a judge with six? {name}, pick one and tell me why. Here's my answer: I'll take the adjuster every time, because the judge's page is the one that can't be argued with. This is the Scheduling Order, entered 12/10/2026, and it now runs John Doe's case to a 09/13/2027 trial calendar. A Scheduling Order is the judge's calendar for the case: every big deadline, from experts to trial, in one order nobody gets to ignore. Every date in it is absolute. So how do we make sure none of them sneaks up on us? Two tools. A trial-prep checklist turns each date into a task somebody owns. And KPIs, which are just measurable scores, prove week by week that each task is ahead of its deadline. The order sets the dates, the checklist assigns them, and the numbers show we're winning the race. And there's one KPI on this list that most firms never track, and it's the one that saves trials. Stay with me.
why.ask: {name}, why does one page signed by a judge outrank every adjuster letter in this file?

theory.say: Four ideas, in plain words. Trial preparation is gathering the final pieces so Atty. Thorne walks into court fully armed. Discovery is the heavy lifting, both sides showing their cards, and it's where most of your time goes. A deposition is an interview under oath, recorded by a court reporter, and you own the logistics, never the testimony. And because a lawsuit can take one to three years, we rerun the records and bills, so the jury sees the total cost of the injury, not the snapshot from before suit. To keep it all honest, we run a weekly KPI audit, like a process server assigned within 48 hours. Speaking of records: request them by subpoena and some custodian will call you back to say they've “never heard of” a patient who was there for three months. That's why we track everything with a date, {name}. Proof beats memory.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four have you already seen show up on John Doe's file, and where?

frame.say: Phase three comes down to three jobs. First guess, {name}: which one do attorneys complain about most when it's done badly? First, the final run. You rerun records from every provider, and you never just reuse the package from before suit, because a year-old record tells a year-old story. Second, subpoena management. A subpoena is the court's order that makes someone produce records or show up. You draft trial subpoenas for the witnesses Atty. Thorne names. You don't pick the witnesses; he does. Third, the trial binder. You index and tab every exhibit so, at the counsel table, he can put his hand on any document in seconds. And the answer is the binder. I watched an attorney once flip through an untabbed binder in front of a jury for almost a full minute. The jury noticed. The lazy binder is a stack. The high-value binder is a map.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file today, which of these three jobs is already in motion?

rules.say: The Scheduling Order controls. Pin it to the front of the file with 30-, 14- and 7-day alerts on every date: our experts 03/15/2027, theirs 04/15/2027, mediation by 03/31/2027, discovery closing 05/28/2027, pretrial 08/12/2027 and trial calendar 09/13/2027. Every extension goes in writing: once Atty. Thorne agrees, you draft the same-day confirmation for his signature, in his name. Watch two traps. One is treating court deadlines like adjuster deadlines. The other is letting the client talk to the other side; if Keystone or a defense investigator reaches John Doe, step in and tell Atty. Thorne that day. For the 02/18/2027 deposition, you handle the reporter, the link, the tech check and the packet by 02/11/2027. Prepare the process, never the testimony. And here's that KPI I promised: every KPI gets a formula and a target, because “stay on top of it” isn't a measure. {name}, that's the one most firms skip.
rules.ask: {name}, defense counsel will spend John Doe's deposition on the 14-Day Gap. What's your job before 02/18/2027, and where does it stop?

model.say: This is what being ahead looks like. {name}, count the milestones with me. Across the top is the runway, from 01/20/2027 to 09/13/2027, with seven of them: the deposition on 02/18, our experts 03/15, mediation by 03/31, defense experts 04/15, discovery closing 05/28, pretrial 08/12 and the trial calendar 09/13. Before each one, three little ticks for the 30, 14 and 7-day alerts. Notice the red band dropping from 05/28: nothing that needs an answer gets scheduled past it. Underneath are nine KPIs in three families, and every one has a target you can measure, like 48 hours, 1 hour, 7 days or 10 days. A KPI without a target is a wish. “Stay on top of RFAs” is a wish. “Every RFA calendared within one hour of receipt” is a KPI. And a file that hits its targets is a file the defense can't catch napping, which is exactly what brings a better number at mediation.
model.ask: {name}, how would you rewrite “stay on top of RFAs” so it actually becomes a KPI?

job.say: A week in the life. The Scheduling Order is entered 12/10/2026. You pin it to the file, calendar all six dates with three alerts each, that's 18 alerts, and file the order in 01_PLEADINGS. Then Atty. Mercer's office calls and an extension gets agreed by phone. The lazy move is “great, we're good.” The high-value move: you confirm Atty. Thorne actually approved it, draft the written confirmation for his signature, send it that same day in his name, and recalendar. No Scheduling Order date moves without a court order. A Case Manager I knew once trusted a handshake extension. Opposing counsel “didn't recall” it three weeks later. Then the deposition is noticed. You book the reporter, the link and the tech check, and send the attorney-approved packet by 02/11/2027, confirming John Doe got it. Every week you run the docket audit, every KPI with its formula, target and dated reading, and every miss gets routed.
job.ask: {name}, opposing counsel says “we'll paper the extension later.” What do you send, and when?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues, one at a time, each a snapshot from John Doe's litigation file. Call it, Do or Don't, then name the rule. Call early if you're confident, but if you're wrong, the room steals it. {name}, keep score. {name}, you're first up. The rules in play: three alerts on every order date, the 30-day client call, the 10-day subpoena audit, who chooses trial witnesses, setting John Doe's expectations, phone-only extensions, old records, and late prep packets. While you play: the bare-minimum file has the dates. The high-value file has the dates, the owners, the alerts and the proof each one was met. Now your mystery. On the trial-prep checklist you'll audit later today, at least one date was copied from the calendar before it was corrected. {name}, your challenge is to spot it faster than anyone in the room.
dodont.ask: {name}, who do you think can call this one on the very first clue?

case.say: It's 01/05/2027, Track B, the road where the case went to suit. Quick bet before I show you anything: {name}, how many mistakes do you think a three-month-old Pleadings Log can collect if nobody checks it? Guess a number. Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417 is three months old. The docket calendar was audited and corrected on 12/10/2026, but nobody reconciled the CMS Pleadings Log to it, and the check now shows five mismatches. The executed Affidavit of Service, filed 10/16/2026, is still sitting in an Allied Process Services email with no row. That's the process server's sworn statement that Smith was handed the lawsuit, our only proof he was served. The Interrogatories and RFPs mailed 12/01/2026 share one row that still says due 12/31/2026, while the calendar shows 01/04/2027. There's no row at all for the 15 RFAs. The Scheduling Order is saved as scan_1210.pdf, and a Certificate of Service dated 01/04/2027 sits in Documents, unlogged. That's our signed line saying when and how we sent papers to the other side. If you've ever named a file scan_1210, don't worry, we've all got one. Ninety seconds, find what's wrong.
case.ask: {name}, in ninety seconds, how many problems can you find in this log as it stands?

task.say: Here's your job. Repair the Pleadings Log and Discovery Calendar for 26-CV-04417, working in CMS under Litigation, Calendar and Documents. Add every missing row, recompute each response date from its trigger and its method of service, and write the math right into the row. File each document in its numbered sub-folder with a proper name, and calendar the Scheduling Order's six dates. Then the graded call: the RFA deadline never had its own row, and it's passed. Prove compliance from that Certificate of Service, record the misses honestly, and report to Atty. Thorne today. Partway through, Jenna Price, Atty. Mercer's paralegal, will call. Log her words exactly, with the time, take no position, tell her only that Atty. Thorne will respond, and route it to him. {name}, you're on the Certificate. {name}, you're on the RFA row. The lazy fix hides the miss. The high-value fix shows it, with the proof.
task.ask: {name}, the log said 12/31/2026, which was too early. Why fix a date that could only have made us early?

check.say: Before you log this, check row by row, and I'm calling on people. {name}, is there an affidavit row, personal service 10/14/2026 by Allied Process Services, filed 10/16/2026, saved in 02_SERVICE_DOCS? Did you correct the Interrogatories and RFPs to 01/04/2027 with the count written out: 12/01 plus 30, plus 3 for mail, Sunday rolled to Monday? The 15 RFAs need their own row with a red deemed-admission flag. Is the Certificate of Service logged and checked, signed verification attached? Smith's responses go on 01/13/2027, with no extra 3 days for e-service on this file. E-service just means papers sent electronically, and whether it adds days depends on the court's rules, which Atty. Thorne confirms. The Scheduling Order renamed, filed in 01_PLEADINGS, all six dates in. And the late rows recorded as misses, not back-dated. Back-dating is the one thing that turns a mistake into a problem nobody can fix. Here's your mystery for the next activity: one date on the trial-prep checklist is still from the old calendar. {name}, hunt it down.
check.ask: {name}, be honest: did anyone add three mail days to the e-served set out of habit?

case.say: It's 01/20/2027, and a notice just landed. {name}, before I read it, guess what's being scheduled. Here it is: John Doe's deposition, 02/18/2027, 10:00 a.m., by videoconference, with Riverton Court Reporting. The link comes from the reporter, and they want us to confirm attendance. Now the problem. Our trial-prep checklist was drafted from the calendar as first keyed, before the 12/10/2026 audit, and never reconciled. It shows our expert disclosure on 04/15/2027, lists mediation 03/31/2027 as if that's the session date, plans records subpoenas for June 2027, and sources the final records run from the old Demand Package. There are no alerts and no deposition tasks. Smith's responses came in 01/13/2027 and were never docketed, and there's no KPI tracker at all. A checklist that's wrong is worse than no checklist, because people trust it. Put it beside the Scheduling Order and find the first wrong date.
case.ask: {name}, can you find the first wrong date in under a minute?

task.say: Here's what you'll do. In the CMS, audit the checklist line by line against the 12/10/2026 Scheduling Order. Every date right, every task with an owner, and each with 30-, 14- and 7-day alerts. Add the 02/18/2027 deposition logistics and the prep document set. Then build the KPI tracker in CMS under Litigation: all nine KPIs, each with its formula and target, this file's reading with its source, and met, missed or open. Close with one task each for the three review lenses: coverage, treatment and liability. Think of them as three pairs of glasses: is there money to pay, is the care documented and on track, and can we prove who caused the crash? {name}, you're on the dates. {name}, you're on the KPIs. The graded call is choosing which two items go to Atty. Thorne first. And just so you know, e-filing portals have a sixth sense for the moment you're in a hurry. Build your alerts so you're never filing at 11:59 p.m. The bare-minimum checklist has tasks. The high-value one has owners, alerts and proof.
task.ask: {name}, which two items go to Atty. Thorne first, and why those two?

model.say: Here's the reference model, and {name}, count the corrections with me as we go. On the left is the checklist with its faulty lines numbered. Our experts on 04/15/2027 get struck through and corrected to 03/15/2027. Mediation 03/31 becomes completed by 03/31. The records subpoenas get dragged back from June across the red 05/28/2027 cutoff, the final records run is re-sourced from the providers, and the blank deposition block fills in. On the right is the KPI tracker, five columns: KPI, formula, target, reading and status, with green, red and amber chips. Each corrected checklist line connects to the KPI it moves. And in the corner, the line I want you to remember: no record means not done. Why does this matter so much? Because a subpoena served in June, after discovery closes, brings back records the jury may never see. One wrong month can cost John Doe his best evidence.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think each corrected checklist line is tied to a specific KPI?

check.say: Check before you log it. {name}, our expert date should now read 03/15/2027, with 04/15/2027 kept as the defense date. Mediation says completed by 03/31/2027. Records subpoenas return before 05/28/2027, and 04/28/2027 is flagged as the last day to e-serve a 30-day request, confirmed with Atty. Thorne. All six dates carry three alerts, 18 in all. The deposition notice is docketed by 01/22/2027, the reporter confirmed, calendars aligned and the packet set for 02/11/2027. Your Gap Record lists the documents, the EMS report, the Northgate attendance, the texts to Margaret, the MRI read, the Causation Letter, and nothing scripted for John Doe. Nine KPIs with formula, target, sourced reading and status. And Smith's 01/13/2027 responses logged as a docket miss and routed. Now your mystery for the Learning Check: John Doe goes quiet before his deposition. {name}, what's your first move, and who hears about it?
check.ask: {name}, is there anything in your Gap Record that tells John Doe what to say?

questions.say: Welcome to the Learning Check, game-show edition. Every answer comes from John Doe's file, in your own words, typed right under the question. {name}, you're our first contestant. Question 1 is the gate, so take it slowly. Work the 12/01/2026 response date step by step, explain how the count changes for a set e-served by consent, meaning both sides agreed in writing to trade papers electronically, and tell me why you'd confirm the court's rule. If your answer is 12/31/2026 or 01/03/2027, that's the buzzer, so stop and rework the count before you go on. Then name Atty. Mercer's three defenses and the evidence on file you'd pull against each, and tell me where the affidavit, the RFAs and the Scheduling Order get filed and named. No phone-a-friend, but you can phone the calendar. And no, the cousin who's “basically a paralegal” doesn't count either.
questions.ask: {name}, before you start, what are the three steps in counting from a mailed trigger?

summary.say: Now the self-summary, in your own words. First, think about this: opposing counsel wants two weeks at 4:45 p.m. and says they'll paper it later. Who can say yes? Only Atty. Thorne, and only in writing, the same day. A Case Manager I trained once said “sure, no problem” on a call like that, to be friendly. Friendly cost us three weeks of arguing. Now your scenario. It's 01/28/2027. John Doe has been unreachable for six days, his deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027, and defense counsel wants to inspect Margaret's Civic. Write your next five actions in order, and next to each one, who owns it. Be specific about what's yours and what goes to Atty. Thorne. The lazy answer is “call John again.” The high-value answer has five steps, five owners, and a reason for the order. {name}, I'll read yours first.
summary.ask: {name}, opposing counsel wants two weeks at 4:45 p.m. and will paper it later. Who can say yes?

scale.say: Last step. Rate yourself on each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll compare your rating with your score, so if you gave yourself a 5 on deadlines but missed the count in Question 1, we'll talk about that gap. It's not a gotcha; it's how we find what to practice next. And remember, UPL, giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer, is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach. Here's your mystery for the Property Damage check coming up next: the Civic's screen had a number untouched since April that was wrong in two directions at once. {name}, can you name it, and both directions, without looking?
scale.ask: {name}, where do you expect the biggest gap between your self-rating and your score?

why.say: Remember the question from Day 1? Does Property Damage touch our case? It's back, and this time money is on the table. Quick true or false, hands up for true. Keystone offering Margaret $792.00 for her Civic lowers John Doe's settlement. {name}, true or false? False. Margaret's Loss of Use and Diminished Value are her own claim, on the separate file the firm opened for her, paid from Keystone's $25,000 Property Damage limit, outside John's $40,000 stack. His numbers don't move. But three things from that file can still reach him: a release worded too widely, the photos and estimates already in his severity set, and the rental dates behind his gap. Our job today is telling which is which, and routing.
why.ask: {name}, of those three, which one could hurt John Doe the most if nobody caught it?

rules.say: The rules, lazy version first. The lazy Case Manager sees a car offer, assumes it has nothing to do with John, and forwards the paperwork to whoever asked. The high-value Case Manager reads the release before the numbers. Keystone's 12/10/2026 release covers all claims arising from the 02/06/2026 accident and asks Mr. Doe to sign. A Property Damage release must never release the injury claim, so you check the claim number, KM-26-440871-PD for the car against KM-26-440871 for John, you hold it, and you route it to Atty. Thorne the same day. John signs nothing. Keep the photos, the estimate and the $2,315.00 supplement identical on both files, and the rental dates too. And never accept, reject, counter or value a car figure.
rules.ask: {name}, the release says Mr. Doe. Which Mr. Doe could sign it, and why does that worry us?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. Keystone sends a release: you check its scope and claim number, hold it, and escalate it to Atty. Thorne in Tasks, and nobody gets asked to sign. Keystone restates its figure: you log it on Margaret's Property Damage file, and John's Net Sheet doesn't change by a penny. Defense counsel asks for the car documents in discovery: you confirm the severity set and the rental dates match the Property Damage file, page by page. I once saw a release signed in a parking lot because the client wanted lunch. Nobody wants that story. A small action today, a release held for one afternoon, protects the whole injury case.
job.ask: {name}, Keystone moves its offer up. What changes on John Doe's Net Sheet?

task.say: Your task has five moves. First, read the release, its scope and its claim number, before you look at a single dollar figure. Second, hold it and route it to Atty. Thorne in Tasks, escalated the same day. Third, sort each outcome: the release, the Diminished Value figure, the Loss of Use figure, the severity set and the rental dates. For each one, does it reach John's settlement or stay on Margaret's file, and why, in one line. Fourth, take Leah Moran's call, and accept nothing, reject nothing, counter nothing. Fifth, write Atty. Thorne a short memo that ends in one line: does this touch John's case, and how? {name}, I'll read yours first.
task.ask: {name}, what will you say when Leah asks if Mr. Doe will just sign today?

case.say: It's 12/10/2026, and an email just landed from Leah Moran at Keystone's Property Damage desk. Before I open it, {name}, guess what's attached. A check? A release. Keystone's final position on Margaret's Civic is $792.00 for Diminished Value and $0 for Loss of Use, and the release covers all claims arising from the 02/06/2026 accident, for Mr. Doe to sign so payment can go out. She's calling this afternoon. Meanwhile John's injury suit is in discovery, and Atty. Thorne wants to know what any of this changes for John. Joke from the job: an adjuster's deadline is always this afternoon, and our answer is always whenever Atty. Thorne decides.
case.ask: {name}, before any math, what's the first thing you check on that release?

check.say: Before you log it, check your work, and I'm picking on a few of you. The release flagged and routed the same day, with nobody asked to sign? The claim numbers checked? Diminished Value and Loss of Use sorted to Margaret's file? John's liens and Net Sheet unchanged, because Keystone's Property Damage money sits outside his stack? The severity set and the rental dates matching both files? Leah told only that it's with Atty. Thorne? The lazy memo lists the numbers. The high-value memo leads with the decision Atty. Thorne has to make and ends with the answer. {name}, read me your last line.
check.ask: {name}, when Leah asked whether he'd take it, what exactly did you say?

questions.say: Property Damage transition, game-show style. Every answer from John Doe's file, in your own words, right under each question. First, Keystone's release covers all claims: why must it never reach John, and what do you do with it? Second, sort Keystone's final position: what reaches John's settlement and what stays on Margaret's file, and why. Third, which car documents already serve John's case, and what has to match on both files? {name}, you're up first, and the buzzer is very sensitive today.
questions.ask: {name}, in one breath: what does $792.00 do to John Doe's Net Sheet?

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary, in your own words. Start with the one line from Day 1, upgraded for settlement: how does Property Damage touch John Doe's case now, and how doesn't it? Then the pressure scenario: Leah wants an answer today and her release is on your desk, so what is your next action, and why that one rather than something else? Last, name the thing you're least sure of. {name}, I'll ask you to read yours, so make it honest.
summary.ask: {name}, what's your next action with the release, and why that one first?

scale.say: Finally, rate yourself on each skill, 1 to 5, and submit it for review. I'll sit your rating next to your score. If you gave yourself a 5 on a block you scored 60 on, we'll talk. If you gave yourself a 2 on something you aced, we'll talk about that too. The skill I'll look at first today is reading a release for its scope, because that's the one that protects John's whole case.
scale.ask: {name}, which skill here did you rate lowest, and what would move it up a point?

why.say: Quick game: true or false, and I want hands. One: the first thing you do when a nervous client calls about his deposition is calm him down. Two: a deposition happens in front of a judge. Three: the Case Manager tells the client what to say. {name}, you're my tiebreaker on number one. Here's the twist: they're all false, and the first one is the sneaky one. Look at the calendar. John resurfaced on 02/03/2027, fifteen days before he testifies on 02/18/2027, by video, from a room the firm doesn't control. Before anybody calms anybody, we audit the file for everything the defense might use, so Atty. Thorne sees it first. A deposition, by the way, is just the other side's lawyer asking John questions under oath, with a court reporter typing every word. Here's the split I want you to hold all module: Atty. Thorne prepares the substance, what John's testimony covers. You prepare the person and the setting. And there's one sentence clients say all the time that can wreck a deposition before it starts. I'll tell you what it is in a minute.
why.ask: {name}, John has fifteen days until he testifies. What has to happen before anyone starts calming him down?

theory.say: Here's the reveal: the sentence is “Don't worry, you'll do great.” Sounds kind. It's a prediction, and predictions aren't ours to make. So let's get the ideas down in plain words. A deposition can shape the whole outcome of a litigated case, meaning one that's gone to court. Atty. Thorne owns the legal strategy. You prepare the client for the process and the nerves. That starts with a landmine audit, which just means reading the file for anything the defense will pounce on, so counsel sees it first. Why? Because consistency is credibility. The defense lines up John's testimony with his signed answers and his records, and any mismatch looks like hiding something. Then there's the TV myth. Clients expect a courtroom drama with somebody yelling “Objection!” and slamming a table. The real thing is a conference room and a laptop. And the defense lawyer writes a report to the insurance company on how John will come across to a jury. {name}, that report is basically a review of John, and it moves the money.
theory.ask: {name}, who reads that defense evaluation report, and why should it worry us?

frame.say: Before I walk through the steps, {name}, guess which one causes the most panic on deposition day. Hold it. First, the pre-deposition audit: prior medical history, signed answers and public social media, with any landmines sent to Atty. Thorne. Then three pillars. Pillar one, de-escalate: no judge, no jury, no shouting, and you calm the client with how the process works, never with a prediction. Pillar two, testimony guidelines: pause, tell the truth, stop once the question's answered, practised only on neutral questions. Pillar three, dress and demeanor: business casual, nothing flashy, limitations described plainly, never shrunk or stretched. I once had a client ask if he could wear his lucky jersey. On video. Of his fantasy football team. Business casual, my friend. Then the technology check: computer, camera at eye level, light in front, quiet private room. And the day before, you confirm the date, time and link with the client, Atty. Thorne and the court reporter. The answer to my guess? The tech. More depositions start late over a frozen camera than over any question.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these steps is already done on John's file, and which is still waiting?

rules.say: Now the rules, lazy version first. The lazy Case Manager sends John a link and says “good luck.” The high-value Case Manager finishes the audit before 02/04/2027 and routes every landmine to Atty. Thorne: the 14-Day Gap, the 19-day disruption, the three 2021 low-back chiropractic visits, the seatbelt and the degenerative MRI. You check John's signed answers and his public social media, and any mismatch goes up the same day. Never tell him to delete a post, because deleting can look worse than the post. His account matches his records because he reviewed them with Atty. Thorne, not because he memorised a script. Then the pillars: calm with the process, pause two seconds, tell the truth, stop talking, business casual, plain about limitations. Test the setup with him on 02/16/2027, confirm with all three parties on 02/17/2027, and nobody in the room, no notes, no messages, not even to you. Why so strict? Because one surprise on the record can cost more at settlement than a month of good treatment earned.
rules.ask: {name}, John asks what he should say about the two weeks before urgent care. What do you tell him?

model.say: Picture two lanes running toward 02/18/2027 at 10:00 a.m. Before I explain them, {name}, guess which direction the arrows on this slide point. Up, down, or both? Across the top are the dates: the audit, then 02/04, 02/11, 02/16, 02/17 and the deposition itself. The upper lane is Atty. Thorne's, labelled substance. The lower lane is yours: the person and the setting. A solid red line divides them. And here's the reveal: the arrows only go one way, upward. Every one is a question routed to him. Nothing comes back down into your lane as content. Down in the corner is John's laptop setup: camera at eye level, light in front, private room, no notes, no messaging. Camera at eye level matters more than you'd think. I've seen a client testify for an hour with the camera pointed straight up his nose. The court reporter never looked at him the same way. Your lane is full of real work, and none of it is what John should say.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the arrows on this slide only ever cross the red line upward?

job.say: Here's how the two weeks really run. The notice of deposition, which is the formal paper saying when and where John testifies, is served 01/20/2027. The lazy move is one calendar entry that says “depo.” The high-value move is calendaring the deposition, both prep sessions, the 02/11/2027 packet and the day-before checklist, so 02/04, 02/11, 02/16, 02/17 and 02/18 at 10:00 a.m. are on the calendar for Atty. Thorne and John. When the audit's done, you route the landmine list and any discovery mismatch to Atty. Thorne before 02/04/2027, every landmine tied to its source record. On 02/16/2027 you run the test call on John's own device, in the room he'll use, and log camera, audio, link, lighting, room and backup number, each pass or fail. On 02/17/2027 you confirm with all three and get the exhibit set approved by Atty. Thorne. {name}, here's why this matters: the defense writes that evaluation report the same week. A calm, prepared John is a bigger number on the other side's spreadsheet.
job.ask: {name}, on the test call, which item would you check first, and why that one?

dodont.say: Game time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues, revealed one at a time, all from John's deposition prep. Call it Do or Don't as soon as you're sure, then name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, you're keeping score. {name}, you're on the first buzz. You'll lean on everything we just covered: consistency is credibility, a calm client gives cleaner answers, everyone gets the dress-code talk, and the traps are surprise records, reassuring predictions, a bad video setup and over-coaching. One warning: some of these clues sound kind and helpful right up until the third one. Kindness that's really a prediction is still a Don't. And here's your mystery for the rest of today: somewhere on John's file is a single word the defense will try to get him to agree with. It sounds harmless, and it isn't. Find it before the next lesson tells you.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's the difference between calming John with the process and calming him with a prediction?

why.say: Let's play a game called Don't Take the Bait. I'm defense counsel, you're the witness, and you only win by not falling for it. Ready? “So it was just the neck stiffness. Is that all?” Hands up if you'd say yes. {name}, I saw that hand. Now look at the 02/20/2026 urgent-care note: hand numbness. That one yes just fenced off a symptom. Atty. Mercer doesn't need John to lie. A hurried yes to a short list, a guess or an argument does the same damage. His Answer and the records tell us exactly where he'll dig: the gap, the disruption, the 2021 visits and the seatbelt. And remember the mystery from last lesson, the harmless word? Here it is: degenerative. If John agrees his neck is just “degenerative,” meaning worn down by age, he's handed the defense a reason the crash didn't cause his pain. What protects him from every one of these traps? Seven general rules and Atty. Thorne's objections. A script protects him from none of them.
why.ask: {name}, be honest: would you have said yes when I asked whether that was all?

theory.say: The defense has a simple goal in a deposition: get the client to contradict himself, lose his temper or exaggerate, because each one damages his credibility. General rules protect against that; a script can't. So let's reset some expectations. Defense counsel may ask very broad questions, and wide questions are normal, not attacks. There's a real difference between an estimate and a guess. An estimate rests on what you saw or felt; a guess claims what you couldn't know, and only the estimate is honest testimony. A deposition is information gathering, not a battle. Nothing gets won there, so the smallest target protects the case. And when Atty. Thorne objects, that's a formal flag on the record protecting the witness, not a sign of trouble. Here's the over-sharer problem in one story. A client of ours was asked, “What time did you leave the house?” He answered with the time, his breakfast, his feud with the neighbor's dog, and the fact that he'd had “maybe one beer the night before.” Nobody asked about the beer. {name}, which rule would have saved him?
theory.ask: {name}, can you give me an honest estimate about John's crash that wouldn't be a guess?

frame.say: These are the seven Golden Rules for testifying. Before I reveal them, {name}, guess which one clients break most often. Hold it. Rule one, always tell the absolute truth, because a damaged case can be saved and a lied-about one can't. Rules two and three: pause two full seconds, then answer in words. That gives time to think, a clean transcript and a window for Atty. Thorne to object. Rules four and five: never guess, and answer only what was asked, then stop. “I don't know” is a complete answer, and it keeps the target small. Rules six and seven: hold the silence after you've answered, and don't try to win. And the answer to my guess is rule five. Every lawyer in America has said “just answer the question” so many times it should be printed on their business cards. These are general rules. We teach every client the same seven, and none of them tells John what to say.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these seven do you think John will find hardest under pressure?

rules.say: Now the rules on the job, lazy versus excellent. The lazy Case Manager hands John the seven rules on a sheet and says “read this.” The excellent one knows where the traps sit on this file. Defense questions come in four categories: personal background, crash mechanics, medical history and daily life. Clients underreport medical history most, and here that's the 2021 low-back visits. Rule one is the truth, and the prior-injury question is the Liar's Trap; counsel usually has the records already. Pause two seconds and answer in words, since the court reporter can't type a nod. Never guess, answer only what's asked, then hold the silence and don't argue. The “Is that all” trap can fence off the hand numbness, and the complete record, not memory, is the full list. Compound questions fold two facts into one yes, and John can say a question's unclear. On an objection, John stops, then answers unless he's told not to. The EMS report, MRI and EDR are Atty. Thorne's to use. You explain rules; you never coach answers.
rules.ask: {name}, which category do clients underreport, and where does that sit on John's file?

model.say: This is the trap map for John's file. {name}, before I walk it, count the traps on the left and tell me how many there are. Seven: Is that all, the compound question, degenerative, the gap mischaracterised, the seatbelt, the 2021 prior and the silent stare. In the centre are the seven rules: truth, pause, say it in words, no guessing, keep it short, hold the silence, don't argue. Each trap connects to the rule that meets it. And every one of those connections ends on the right, in one tall shield: Atty. Thorne, who prepares and objects. Now notice what's missing. There's no scripted answer anywhere on this slide, and that empty space is on purpose. The silent stare is my favourite. Defense counsel just looks at you after you answer, and the silence gets so loud the witness starts talking to fill it. I've seen a client break the silence by asking the lawyer where he bought his tie. Along the bottom is the habit for John: when there's an objection, stop talking.
model.ask: {name}, which rule meets the silent stare, and why does that one rattle clients so much?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. Atty. Mercer's Answer, the defense's formal reply to our lawsuit, was served 11/12/2026. You take each defense it pleads, comparative fault, causation and failure to mitigate, and map it to the questions it predicts in the deposition prep log, so each one ties to at least one trap. Once the trap map's done, you check that the record meeting each trap is actually in Atty. Thorne's set: the EMS report, the MRI report of 03/13/2026, the 06/19/2026 Causation Letter, the EDR download and the Northgate Attendance Record. And when John asks you how to answer one of those traps, and he will, you log his question in his own words and route it to Atty. Thorne the same day. No wording offered, not even a little. Why so careful? Because if the defense can show the Case Manager fed John his answers, his whole testimony looks rehearsed, and a rehearsed witness is worth less at the settlement table. {name}, you'll feel the pull to help. Help by routing.
job.ask: {name}, John asks you, “How should I answer the seatbelt question?” What exactly do you do next?

dodont.say: Game time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule, for opposing counsel's traps. I'll reveal three clues one at a time. Call it, Do or Don't, then name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score, and {name}, you're first on the buzzer. You'll need what we just built: a deposition is information gathering and the records win later, we explain objections ahead of time, silence is safe and rambling isn't, and the traps are a narrowed yes, a client who argues or talks over an objection, and prep that skips the medical history. Some of these clues will sound like John is doing great. Listen for the moment it turns. And your challenge for the rest of today: when you run John's first prep session, he's going to ask you five questions that sound like logistics but aren't. Count them as they come, and see if you can catch all five before I do.
dodont.ask: {name}, can you name the Golden Rule behind this one, not just the call?

case.say: It's 02/04/2027 on Track B, the road where John Doe's case is in a lawsuit. Before I tell you what just landed, {name}, guess: after twelve days of silence, how do you think we finally reached John? Here's the reveal. John Doe went dark on 01/22/2027, and yesterday we reached him through Margaret. He has a new phone number. His deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027 at 10:00 a.m., by videoconference with Riverton Court Reporting, and he's anxious; he's expecting a TV cross-examination with somebody pacing in front of a jury box. Atty. Thorne's note says prep session one is at 1:00 p.m. and you open it: the new number, the logistics, the test call, the three pillars and the room rules. He'll listen, then take the substance, and he wants John's gap set ready to share on screen. One thing before we start. What decides your grade is the routing. A polished segment that answers even one substantive question fails. Clients ask the big question in the smallest voice, usually right as you're saying goodbye, with “oh, one quick thing.”
case.ask: {name}, what's the very first thing you'll update in the CMS before the session starts?

task.say: Here's your job. You'll run your segment of John's first prep session in the Call Simulator with AI John Doe. Confirm his new number, with Margaret as backup. State the logistics exactly and set a 02/16/2027 test call on the device and in the room he'll use. Deliver the three pillars and the room rules in plain words, and practise the two-second pause on neutral questions only, like “What's your name?” Now, remember my challenge, the five questions that sound like logistics but aren't? Here they come. AI John will ask what to say about the gap, the missed April therapy, the seatbelt, his 2021 chiropractor visits and the MRI. Recognise each as substance, answer none, and log each in his words to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate. Have the gap set ready to share. {name}, you're up first. {name}, you're tracking how many of the five your classmate catches. You hand in your segment, a logistics record and John's routed questions.
task.ask: {name}, which of John's questions can you answer, and which ones can't you?

model.say: So what does a good segment look like? John's tile is big on the video call, yours sits beside it, and Atty. Thorne is small in the corner, listening. Under the call is your agenda, five steps: logistics, calm, guidelines, dress and demeanor, and the room rules. On the right is the card that matters most: routed to Atty. Thorne, with five lines for the gap, the disruption, the seatbelt, the 2021 visits and the MRI. As John asks, those lines fill up. And here's the reveal: your answers to them stay empty, every time. The dress talk, by the way, is advice every client gets. I once had a client show up to a video deposition in a full tuxedo, bow tie and all, because his cousin told him “dress like it's important.” He wasn't wrong, he was just three levels too important. The message across the bottom says it all: answer the process, route the substance. {name}, look at that empty answer column. That's what a perfect score looks like.
model.ask: {name}, if John pushes a second time on the gap, what keeps that answer line empty?

check.say: Before you log your segment, check yourself, and I'm going to pick on a few of you. {name}, is his new number updated in the CMS under Parties, with Margaret confirmed as backup? Did you state the logistics exactly, 02/18/2027, 10:00 a.m., videoconference, Riverton Court Reporting, and set the 02/16/2027 test call? Did you explain the setting without predicting any outcome, practise the pause on neutral questions only, and give the dress talk as advice every client gets? Did you cover the room rules: private room, no one else, no notes, no phone, no messaging? And the big one: all five substantive questions met with routing, not content, each logged in John's words before the segment ended. The lazy segment sounds helpful. The high-value segment is helpful and safe. Watch the helpful half-answer. “Always tell the truth” is a rule; “just say you had no ride” is a script. And here's your mystery for the mock: on 02/16, one trap is going to work on John. Your log decides whether Atty. Thorne can fix it.
check.ask: {name}, did anything you said today sound like “just say you had no ride”?

case.say: It's 02/16/2027, the second prep session. At 2:00 p.m., Atty. Thorne is running a mock cross-examination, which is a practice round where someone plays the other side's lawyer. Quick poll before I give you your role: hands up if you think you'll get to talk during this one. {name}, put that hand down slowly. Let me set the roles out loud, because the boundary matters. Atty. Thorne leads and defends. AI defense counsel, playing Atty. Grant Mercer, asks the questions. AI John Doe answers. And you observe. Your microphone stays muted the whole time. Your job is the Trap Log: every trap with its time, Mercer's exact words, and the record fact beside any mischaracterisation, plus every objection. Atty. Thorne debriefs John from your log when the mock ends, so it has to reach him before we finish. Muting yourself sounds easy. It isn't. Every Case Manager I've trained has, at least once, nodded so hard at a good answer the camera caught it.
case.ask: {name}, who in this mock is allowed to speak to John, and when?

task.say: While the mock runs in the Call Simulator, you keep the Trap Log in the CMS under Litigation, Deposition prep log. For each trap, log the timestamp, the question in AI Mercer's exact words, its category, the trap type, and which Golden Rules John kept or broke. Beside every mischaracterisation, meaning the lawyer describing a fact the wrong way, put the record fact and its source. Log each objection and whether John stopped talking. Then route the finished log to Atty. Thorne before his debrief. You coach nothing, not during the mock and not after. The log is for Atty. Thorne alone; nothing in it goes to John. The lazy log says “he asked about the gap, John did okay.” The high-value log says what was asked, word for word, at what minute, and what the record actually shows. {name}, you're logging the first half. {name}, you take the second. Your hand-in is a timestamped Trap Log, scored against the seven rules.
task.ask: {name}, why does the log need Mercer's exact words instead of your summary of the question?

model.say: Here are two entries from a model Trap Log. {name}, before I zoom in, tell me what you'd expect to see in a perfect entry. On the left is the mock: AI Mercer questioning, AI John answering, and Atty. Thorne's tile flagged for an objection, with a running timer up top. On the right is the log itself, with columns for the time, the question as asked, the category, trap and record, and the rules. Above it sit the trap chips, turning orange as each one gets logged, with the silent stare dashed because Mercer may not use it. And look at your own tile at the bottom, microphone struck through. Across the foot it says observe, log, route, never coach. Your only output in this exercise is the log. I once watched a client answer a simple seatbelt question with “I always wear it, unlike everybody else on that road.” Nobody asked about everybody else. Everyone in a crash is sure the other guy was the problem, and it shows up on the record every time.
model.ask: {name}, looking at these two entries, what makes each one useful for Atty. Thorne's debrief?

check.say: Check your log before you route it. {name}, are all six traps there, plus the silent stare if Mercer used it, each with a timestamp, his exact words and one of the four categories? Your gap entry should read 14 days, 02/06/2026 to 02/20/2026, and any disruption question set against 19 days, 04/02/2026 to 04/21/2026. Degenerative should cite the 03/13/2026 MRI: no significant degenerative change at the adjacent levels. The seatbelt entry cites the EMS Run Report and the EDR download, and the 2021 entry notes three resolved low-back visits and no prior neck complaints. Each answer scored on the rules, every objection logged. Why the precision? Because every mischaracterisation you catch today is one Atty. Thorne can correct before 02/18, and one less line in the defense's evaluation report. And honestly: did you nod, type in the chat, or say anything to John? That's coaching, in a mock or on 02/18/2027. Your mystery for the Learning Check: one trap is the one clients fall for most. Name it, and prove it from the file.
check.ask: {name}, which trap worked on John, and which rule would have protected him?

questions.say: This is the Deposition Readiness Audit, and we're playing it like a game show. Look at the readiness strip on screen first. {name}, which chip is hardest to turn green honestly? Most people say the audit. I'd say the routing, because it's the one that gets tested under pressure, usually by a client who says “I'm not asking for legal advice, I just want to know what you'd say.” That's legal advice wearing a fake moustache. Now answer from John's file, in your own words, under each question. List the landmines your audit must surface before 02/04/2027, with the record behind each. Lay out the day-before checklist for 02/17/2027. And name the four categories of defense questions, the one clients underreport, and where that risk sits here. That's the mystery from the mock, by the way: the trap clients fall for most lives in that underreported category. {name}, you're first to share when we review.
questions.ask: {name}, which chip on the readiness strip is hardest to turn green honestly?

summary.say: On to your self-summary. Warm-up first, and {name}, you're answering. It's 02/03/2027, and John has just resurfaced with a new phone, fifteen days before he testifies. What can't wait? His new number in the CMS, and the audit routed to Atty. Thorne. The lazy Case Manager says “great, he's back” and goes to lunch. The high-value one updates Parties before the call even ends. Keep that urgency in mind. Then write your scenario: it's 01/28/2027, John's been unreachable for six days, his deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027, and defense counsel wants to inspect Margaret's Civic. Give me your next five actions in order, with an owner beside each one. Every one of those actions protects the same thing: a deposition that goes forward on time, with a client who shows up. A no-show deposition doesn't just cost a day; it hands the defense a story about a client who doesn't care about his own case.
summary.ask: {name}, John just resurfaced fifteen days out. What's the first thing you do before the call ends?

scale.say: Last piece: rate yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, then submit it. I'm going to compare your rating with your score and talk through any wide gaps with you. {name}, no pressure, but I've seen people give themselves a five and then spell “deposition” three different ways in one answer. And let me be straight about Question 5, because it's the UPL gate. UPL means the unauthorized practice of law, a non-lawyer giving legal advice. Any reply that gives John content about the gap fails the module, however polished it is. The right reply routes his question to Atty. Thorne and logs it in John's words. Rate yourself with that in mind. And your mystery for the final check: $20,359.92. That's a real number from John's file, to the cent. Before the next Learning Check, work out where it comes from, because you'll be asked to rebuild it deduction by deduction.
scale.ask: {name}, where would you honestly rate your routing under pressure right now?

why.say: Quick game: Whose Fault Is It Anyway? I'll read you three things Robert Smith's Answer says, and you shout “John” if it's about John's own conduct and “Not John” if it isn't. One: the Escape entered the all-way stop out of turn. Two: John was unbelted. Three: John failed to mitigate by missing visits. {name}, you call the first one. Here's the reveal: number one isn't about John at all. Entering out of turn is about Kevin Alvarez's driving. After suit, the defense went after fault and mitigation. The seatbelt is comparative fault, which means blaming John for part of his own injuries. The missed visits are failure to mitigate, which means saying he didn't do enough to get better. And here's the difference that matters. Fault can reduce or even wipe out recovery. Mitigation only cuts the damages the missed care actually caused. Funny thing about crashes: I've never once met a driver who thought it was their fault. Ten cars, ten witnesses, ten people sure it was the other guy. That's why we answer every allegation with a document, not an opinion.
why.ask: {name}, which of Smith's three allegations isn't about John's own conduct at all?

theory.say: Before I give you the ideas, {name}, guess: if a jury says John is 20% at fault, does he always get 80% of his damages? Hold that. Comparative negligence splits fault between the people involved, and the share charged to the injured person can reduce, or even bar, what they recover. There are three systems, pure, modified and contributory, and they treat the very same finding differently. So it's the state's rule, not the percentage alone, that decides the money. The answer to my guess: not always. Next, liability status: accepted, partial or denied, recorded with its source, so Atty. Thorne sees what's still being fought over. And keep fault and mitigation in separate boxes. Comparative fault is about the crash. Failure to mitigate is about later care, and it only trims damages that could have been avoided. All of this feeds the counter-package, which is just an index that answers each defense claim with evidence that can actually be used in court.
theory.ask: {name}, why doesn't the percentage of fault, on its own, tell us what John recovers?

frame.say: Here's the counter-package laid out, one allegation per row. Entered the stop out of turn: that's about Kevin Alvarez's driving, and Ruth Calloway, the doorbell video and the point of impact answer it, with the EDR corroborating. Unbelted passenger: that's about John's seatbelt, and the EDR shows the belt buckled while the EMS report reads restrained front-seat passenger. Failure to mitigate: the 19 days without visits, 04/02 to 04/21/2026, answered by the A-C-T record and its documented cause, the anxiety after the crash, in Dr. Reyes's 04/20 note and the counselor's 06/10 summary. And causation, the 14-Day Gap and the degenerative MRI, answered by the Gap Record: four reasons, the EMS neck complaint and the Causation Letter. Every allegation, a document.
frame.ask: {name}, which row on John's file do you think the defense will lean on hardest?

rules.say: Now the rules. Comparative negligence splits fault. Under pure, damages fall by John's share, however large. Under modified, they fall, but recovery is barred at 50% in some states or 51% in others. Under contributory, any fault at all bars recovery. Confirm the governing rule with Atty. Thorne. Record liability status with its source; Keystone accepted PD liability on 02/17/2026, and the Answer now pleads comparative fault. The out-of-turn allegation targets Kevin Alvarez, and whatever the defense says about him, the stack stays $40,000. Unbelted is answered by the EDR and the EMS report. Failure to mitigate trims only avoidable damages, and the A-C-T record answers it. Evidence counts only if it can come in, which means it's allowed in court, so record source, witness and custody, meaning who held it and when. Don't rest on the citation alone. You gather and index; Atty. Thorne decides fault, admissibility and coverage. {name}, here's why this matters: every point of fault we can't answer comes straight out of John's check.
rules.ask: {name}, if a jury finds John 20% at fault, what does he recover under each of the three systems?

model.say: One finding, four outcomes. Before I show you the red cells, {name}, guess how many of them say Barred. On the left is the system table, with two columns: John at 20% and John at 50%. Your eye goes straight to the red cells, the ones that say Barred, and that's on purpose. Under contributory, he's barred either way. Under a modified 50% rule, he's barred at 50%. That's the cliff. One percentage point, and a whole recovery falls off it. On the right are the three allegations, each pointing to its answer already in the file. Out of turn: RPD-26-018842, Calloway and the video. Unbelted: EDR buckled and EMS restrained. Failed to mitigate: the A-C-T record from 04/08 to 04/23. And along the bottom, a reminder: the stack stays $40,000. Every point of fault costs John money, and each point already has its answer. That's what a week of careful logging buys you.
model.ask: {name}, under the modified 50% rule, what happens to John's recovery at exactly 50%?

job.say: Watch how it unfolds on the job. The Answer is filed on 11/12/2026, pleading comparative fault, causation and failure to mitigate. You log each defense as its own line in the Pleadings Log, dated 11/12/2026, and confirm the filing on the docket, which is the court's official list of everything filed in the case. Then you map the file's evidence to each allegation in the counter-package, with its source, witness and custody, and nothing goes in without a source document and a named witness who can vouch for it. When an item lacks foundation, or a holder won't hand it over, you flag it for a Subpoena Duces Tecum, a court order to produce documents, and route it to Atty. Thorne, naming the gap and the record holder. With deposition prep set for 02/04 and 02/16/2027, you deliver the counter-package and the Gap Record into his prep set before 02/04/2027. I once saw a perfect piece of evidence get tossed because nobody could say who'd had the USB stick for six months. It was in a desk drawer. Under a sandwich.
job.ask: {name}, why does every item in the counter-package need a named witness and not just a document?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule on the liability counter-package. Three clues, one at a time. Call it, Do or Don't, then give me the rule. {name}, you're keeping score, {name}, you're on the first buzz. Think back over what we just covered: answering each allegation with a document instead of an argument, recording liability status the way the claims team does, using the damage pattern with the video and the witness, and the traps of leaning on the citation alone, promising John he can't be blamed, and adding Kevin Alvarez's policy to the stack. One tip: watch who's speaking in each clue. Sometimes it's not the evidence that's wrong, it's who's giving the opinion. And here's the mystery for the next lesson: two people disappear on this file, months apart. One of them is on our side. Same problem, completely different rules. Come ready to tell me why.
dodont.ask: {name}, who's making the call in that last clue, and should it be them?

why.say: Here's the mystery I left you with: two people went missing on this file. Quick game first. I'll say a clue, you shout “Smith” or “John.” Moved before he could be served. Went silent 27 days before his deposition. Has a mom who answers the phone. {name}, you get the last one. Robert Smith moved before he could be served. John Doe went silent 27 days before his deposition. What do they share? Neither one has a working contact point. What's different? One is the opponent, and one is our client, and who's allowed to do what follows from that. The tools overlap: Skip-Trace, the process server, certified proof of notice. A Skip-Trace is a search of records to find someone's current address. A process server is the person who hands over the court papers. Now, if you've watched TV, you think a skip-trace means a dark room, six monitors and someone yelling “enhance.” In real life it's a database search, a permission form and a lot of waiting. In both cases, the record we keep is what proves we did our job.
why.ask: {name}, Smith and John both went missing. What do they share, and what's different about them?

theory.say: Filing a lawsuit means nothing until service, which is the defendant being formally handed the papers. No service, and the case stalls and can be dismissed. Defendants who know a suit is coming may hide, ignore the door or move, which is why diligent, logged attempts matter: they prove the effort. {name}, guess what a logged failed attempt is worth compared to a successful one. Hold it. When an address goes stale, there's the Skip-Trace, a background search of utility, employment and address records, run only for a permissible purpose, meaning a legal reason the law allows. If someone's still dodging, there's alternative service, a court-approved substitute like mail or posting on the door, and only the attorney can ask for it. On the client side, certified notice gives us proof of mailing, and paired with email, it shows John was told how to respond. And the answer to my guess: almost as much. A failed attempt, logged with date, time and address, is the evidence a judge needs to approve the next step.
theory.ask: {name}, why is a logged failed attempt worth almost as much as a successful one?

frame.say: Here's the evading defendant protocol, step by step. When attempts fail, you log each one's date, time and address and follow up with the server every five days. If the address looks stale, then on Atty. Thorne's authority, a Skip-Trace runs through licensed databases checking utility, employment and active-address records. With the right address and the person still dodging, the server varies the windows, early mornings, evenings and weekends, where the court's rules allow. If that still fails, Atty. Thorne may ask the court to permit alternative service by mail or posting. And when service finally happens, the signed affidavit of service, the server's sworn statement that the papers were delivered, gets filed with the court. Never leave it sitting in an email. The lazy version is “the server's handling it.” The high-value version is knowing every attempt by date and calling the server on day five, not day thirty. {name}, I once had a defendant who answered the door, took the papers, and said “I'm his twin brother.” He wasn't. The server's notes had his tattoo described. Details win.
frame.ask: {name}, on Smith's service, which of these five steps did we actually need?

rules.say: Now the rules, with the real dates. The clerk issues the Summons, the process server gets the papers, you follow up every five days, and the affidavit is filed: here 09/24 filed, 10/14 served, 10/16/2026 affidavit. The Summons, by the way, is the court's official notice telling the defendant he's been sued and how long he has to answer. Three failed attempts at 118 Larkspur Ln and a neighbor saying Smith moved means a stale address, so Skip-Trace first, permissible purpose only. On 10/09 it found 4410 Quarry Ridge Ct, Millbrook. Service starts his clock, answer due 11/13/2026, and you check the docket weekly. A Subpoena Duces Tecum needs a narrow Exhibit A, the list of exactly which records we want, and opposing counsel gets notice first. For John, silent since 01/22/2027, run Day 2's No Contact Protocol, our step-by-step plan for a client who goes quiet, every attempt logged. The Step 4 letter goes certified mail and email over Atty. Thorne's signature, by 01/27/2027. Withdrawal goes in only if he directs it. Margaret hears only that the firm needs John to call. {name}, why so careful with Margaret? Because she's family, not our client, and every extra word to her is a privacy problem.
rules.ask: {name}, three attempts failed at 118 Larkspur Ln. Why is a fourth at 6:00 a.m. the wrong move?

model.say: Same tools, different authority. {name}, before I trace the lanes, tell me which lane you think has the scarier ending. Look at the top lane, Robert Smith, the defendant. Three failed attempts at 118 Larkspur Ln on 10/01, 10/05 and 10/08. Then the Skip-Trace on 10/09 bends the lane to 4410 Quarry Ridge Ct, he's served 10/14, the affidavit follows 10/16, and his answer's due 11/13/2026. Now the bottom lane, John Doe, our client. A silent stretch from 01/22/2027 with the four protocol steps along it, certified mail plus email, and then the break: 02/03, reached through Margaret, ending at the 02/18/2027 deposition. Between the lanes sits the line I want you to remember: withdrawal is never the Case Manager's to raise. Withdrawal, by the way, means the firm stepping away from the case. Clients reappear in the funniest ways. One of mine went silent for a month and resurfaced by replying to a two-week-old email with just “k.” Log the “k.” It's a contact.
model.ask: {name}, looking at both lanes, where does the authority to act change hands?

job.say: Back to October, on the job. On 10/08/2026, the third attempt fails and a neighbor says Smith moved. You escalate for Skip-Trace authority, log the 10/09/2026 result and re-assign the server to 4410 Quarry Ridge Ct. When the affidavit is filed 10/16/2026, you docket the answer date, 11/13/2026, and set a recurring weekly docket check. Later, Atty. Thorne approves a Subpoena Duces Tecum, so you send notice to Atty. Grant Mercer first, dated before service, then have the custodian, the person who keeps the records, served, and set a compliance call five days before production. And when John goes unreachable from 01/22/2027 with a deposition noticed, you run Steps 1 to 3, then draft the Step 4 notice for Atty. Thorne's signature, response date before 02/04/2027, and log both the certified mail and the email. Why does this matter for the money? A defendant who's never served can't be made to pay, and a client who misses his deposition can sink his own case. {name}, both lanes end at the settlement table.
job.ask: {name}, why does opposing counsel get notice of the subpoena before the custodian is served?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule one more time for this lesson. Three clues, one at a time, about finding people on this file. Call it, Do or Don't, and name the rule. {name}, you're scoring, {name}, you're up first. You've got the tools: following up with the server every five days and asking for each attempt's details, paying a custodian's copy invoice the day it arrives, confirming the address before certified mail goes out, and the traps of knocking on a stale door, serving the non-party before opposing counsel has notice, and saying too much to Margaret. Some of these sound like good hustle. Ask yourself whether the hustle is pointed in the right direction. Knocking on the same empty door five times isn't persistence, it's cardio. And here's your mystery for the practice lab: when you get the Skip-Trace return on Smith, it'll list three addresses. Only one of them is real. Your job is to prove which one, with two sources.
dodont.ask: {name}, does working harder at the same address ever count as diligence?

case.say: It's 11/12/2026 on Track B, and something just got filed. {name}, guess: when the other side answers a lawsuit, do they ever just say “yep, our fault”? Me neither, not once in my career. Here's what landed. Atty. Grant Mercer of Mercer & Hale LLP has filed Robert Smith's Answer in Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417. It denies liability and pleads comparative negligence, saying the Escape entered the all-way stop out of turn and John was unbelted. It pleads causation, the gap and a degenerative MRI, and failure to mitigate. Atty. Thorne wants, for each allegation, the evidence that answers it, its source, its authenticating witness, meaning the person who can swear the evidence is what we say it is, and its chain of custody, plus a list of the questions only he can answer. In the file you've got report RPD-26-018842, Ruth Calloway's details, the doorbell video, the 10/2026 EDR download, the EMS Run Report and the A-C-T record. You'll get three blank rows, one per allegation, and I'll grade row by row.
case.ask: {name}, is a row finished if it has strong evidence but no authenticating witness?

task.say: Here's your job. You're building the liability counter-package for Atty. Thorne in the CMS under Litigation. For each of the three allegations, list the evidence that answers it, its source document, the witness who can vouch for it, its chain of custody and any gap in its foundation. Write out the doorbell video's chain from the 02/17/2026 preservation request to the 02/19/2026 copy. Where a record will need a custodian, draft a narrow Exhibit A for a Subpoena Duces Tecum from the firm's template in the CMS, under Documents, for his review. Then close with the questions only he can answer: the governing fault rule, seatbelt and citation admissibility, and whether fault on Kevin Alvarez touches coverage. {name}, you take the out-of-turn row first. {name}, you're on the seatbelt. The lazy package lists evidence. The high-value package lists evidence that can actually walk into a courtroom with a witness holding its hand. You hand in the allegation-by-allegation package, the draft Exhibit A and those routed questions.
task.ask: {name}, which single document answers two of the defenses?

check.say: Check your package against this before you log it. Three separate rows: out of turn, unbelted, failure to mitigate. Out of turn answered by RPD-26-018842, Ruth Calloway of 2209 Maple Hollow Rd, the video and the point of impact, with the EDR's 11 mph as corroboration only, because speed alone doesn't prove right-of-way. Unbelted answered by the EDR and the EMS report. Mitigation answered by the A-C-T record and its clinical cause, with the disruption stated exactly: 19 days, 04/02 to 04/21/2026, four missed visits, crash-related anxiety documented by Dr. Reyes and the counselor. The video's chain runs from Margaret Doe's camera through 02/17 and 02/19/2026, native file unaltered. Every item has a witness. Your Exhibit A covers only John Doe's 02/06/2026 Riverton Fire EMS run and named record types, never all records. And the stack still reads $40,000.
check.ask: {name}, does your Exhibit A name one patient, one date and specific record types?

case.say: Two episodes, one file, and both are disappearing acts. Part one: it's 10/08/2026, and Allied Process Services reports a third failed attempt at 118 Larkspur Ln, tonight at 6:40 p.m., no answer, no vehicle, after tries on 10/01 and 10/05. A neighbor says Robert Smith moved out in August. The server wants to know how to proceed. {name}, before I show you the Skip-Trace return, guess how many addresses come back. Here's the reveal: three. The 10/09 return lists 118 Larkspur Ln with utilities closed 08/2026, 4410 Quarry Ridge Ct, Millbrook, with a utility opened 08/2026 that matches his registration, and a 2019 address. Remember the mystery? Only one is real, and you'll prove which. Part two: it's 01/22/2027, and calls to John go unanswered, two days after his deposition was noticed for 02/18/2027. Prep is set for 02/04 and 02/16/2027. Treat both like a race against a stale address. Neighbors, by the way, are the best investigators in America. They know who moved, when, and what kind of couch went with them.
case.ask: {name}, after the 10/08 report, what's the graded move: a fourth knock, or something else?

task.say: Here's the job, in two parts. In Part one, escalate for Skip-Trace authority through Tasks, Escalate, then evaluate the 10/09 return, choosing the address on recency and two corroborating sources, meaning two separate records that agree, and record why. Re-instruct Allied, log service on 10/14 and the affidavit on 10/16, and docket the answer date. In Part two, run Steps 1 to 3 of the No Contact Protocol with the litigation impact, then draft the Step 4 certified notice, the Final Warning Letter that lists what we tried, sets a deadline and warns we may withdraw, from the firm's template in the CMS, under Documents for Atty. Thorne's signature: attempts itemized, a 7 to 14 day response date before 02/04/2027, how to respond. Send it certified mail and email to a confirmed address. You'll also call Margaret Doe: verify her identity, say only that the firm needs John to call, and log it. Then assess John's Skip-Trace gate. {name}, you're on Smith. {name}, you're on John. The lazy version knocks again and leaves a voicemail. The high-value version can show a judge every step, by date.
task.ask: {name}, John and Smith both have no working contact point. Why does Smith get a Skip-Trace and John doesn't?

check.say: Time for your self-check. {name}, Part one: did you escalate for Skip-Trace after 10/08/2026, not a fourth knock; choose 4410 Quarry Ridge Ct on two current sources and reject 118 Larkspur Ln as stale; log service 10/14/2026, the affidavit 10/16/2026, and docket the answer for 11/13/2026? Part two: Step 1 names the deposition, 27 days out, the prep dates and the 03/15/2027 expert disclosure. Your ladder is logged: calls, email to john.doe@example.com, text, then Margaret. Now check every response date against 02/04/2027. A 14-day window from 01/22 lands on 02/05, one day too late, so it's sent by 01/27/2027 for 02/03/2027. One day. That's how most deadlines get missed, not by a month, by one calendar square. Certified mail to 2214 Maple Hollow Rd and email, signed by Atty. Thorne. No withdrawal language from you, anywhere. And the gate isn't met: John was reached 02/03/2027. Your final mystery: the Final Comprehensive Knowledge Check spans all five days. Which number on this file do you think shows up in it most?
check.ask: {name}, where does your notice's response date fall against the 02/04/2027 prep session?

questions.say: This is the Final Comprehensive Knowledge Check, the last one before Track B's close-out, and it spans all five days. Every answer comes from one file: John Doe's names, dates and figures, not general rules. Before we start, a lightning round, hands up as fast as you can. Who remembers the date of loss? Who remembers the stack total? {name}, you were first, keep that energy. Write in your own words under each question.
