Lay out the Recovery Stack in its order of operations, with each limit and the total, and name three coverages that aren't part of it, then the Payer Order for his Medical Bills. The Recovery Stack is the order the insurance money gets tapped, layer by layer; the Payer Order is who pays which Medical Bill first. Tell me when the window on the 07/20/2026 BI demand closed and why. The BI demand, remember, is our letter asking the at-fault driver's insurer to pay for John Doe's injuries. And reconcile the Track A net of $20,359.92 from $40,000.00, deduction by deduction. There it is: the number from the mystery. Time to prove where it comes from.
questions.ask: {name}, before you start, what's the first layer of John's Recovery Stack?

summary.say: Before you write your self-summary, let's do Question 7 out loud, and {name}, you're answering. John asks you how to explain the gap. What do you say? The only right answer listens, tells him Atty. Thorne will go through it with him, escalates at once and logs the call. Then Question 4, the arithmetic gate: $40,000.00, less the $13,333.33 fee, $486.75 in costs, and the $1,240.00 and $4,580.00 liens, leaves $20,359.92, to the cent. {name}, double-check me on a calculator. Every client checks it, usually twice, usually while asking why the lawyer gets a third. That's the whole week in one number: every lien you logged this week, every reduction, every cost receipt shows up right here. Now your scenario: 01/28/2027, John unreachable for six days, deposition noticed for 02/18/2027, defense counsel asking to inspect the Civic. Your next five actions, in order, with owners.
summary.ask: {name}, John asks how to explain the gap. What do you say, word for word?

scale.say: Last step for the final check. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each competency across all five days, then submit for review. I'll compare your ratings with your scores. Please be honest with yourself here, because this is what we'll coach from. I once had a trainee rate herself five out of five on everything, including “accuracy,” on a form where she'd misspelled her own batch number. We still laugh about it. She's a supervisor now. And know that UPL is a gate, not a weight. A 5 on the UPL competency from someone who coached John in Question 7 doesn't pass, however strong the rest of the paper is. Here's your last challenge before close-out, {name}, and everyone: think back to the very first slide on Day 1. Whose file is it? You've got a much better answer now than you did on Day 1. Bring it to the end-of-day discussion.
scale.ask: {name}, across all five days, which competency surprised you most when you rated it?

why.say: Would you rather, quick round. Hands up: would you rather tell a client their case is being dropped in a letter, or in a phone call? Letter hands up. Phone hands up. {name}, you picked the letter, defend it. Here's the reveal: trick question, because neither of those is your first move. Atty. Thorne talks to the client first, and the letter is never the client's first news. A Dropped Case is a claim the firm stops pursuing before it resolves. John Doe's file never gets here, because earlier today the Skip-Trace found the people his file needed. But some cases do. And a Withdrawal Letter is basically the politest breakup letter ever written: it's not you, it's the case. Done carelessly, a drop leaves a client confused and the firm exposed. Done right, the file proves everyone was told. And there's one sentence in the client's letter that must never appear in the carrier's. I'll tell you which shortly.
why.ask: {name}, if a Dropped Case just went quiet in the CMS with no letters, who could get hurt by that?

theory.say: Vocabulary, in plain words. A Dropped Case is a claim we stop before it's resolved, and it has to be written up, closed out and proved. Cases get dropped for a handful of reasons: the client stops answering or pulls out, we can't show the other driver was at fault, there's no insurance money or not enough of it, the client can't finish treatment, or new facts don't match the old ones. Add one you'll see a lot: a client with no Health Plan who simply can't pay for care. The Withdrawal Letter is the formal notice that the lawyer and client relationship is over. Pending Drop is the status that says the decision's made but the letters haven't gone out yet. And the proof, meaning the receipts, the logs and the saved letters, is what protects the firm later. {name}, think of a file you've seen, at work or on TV. Which of these reasons fits it?
theory.ask: {name}, which of those reasons do you think is the hardest one to explain to a client?

frame.say: Three kinds of recipient, three kinds of letter, and here's the reveal I promised. The client's letter carries the date, the date of loss, the reason in Atty. Thorne's words, and the next step he approves, which is to speak to another attorney promptly. It goes by the client's preferred method, email, text or both, plus Certified Mail, which is mail where the post office gives us proof it was delivered. The carrier's letter carries the date, the client's name, the date of loss and the claim number, and says only that we no longer represent the client. The medical provider's letter says the same and asks them to update their records. Those two go by email or fax, whichever the CRM notes say that party prefers. The CRM is our contact file: who each person is and how they like to be reached. Now look at what's missing from those two letters. The reason. That's the sentence that never travels. {name}, why not?
frame.ask: {name}, what could go wrong if the carrier learned exactly why the firm withdrew?

rules.say: Six steps, always in this order. First, the gate: the status reads Pending Drop, and there's a note from Atty. Thorne or the Case Manager that the client was told. If either is missing, nothing goes out. Second, prepare a Withdrawal Letter for every party on the file, over Atty. Thorne's signature, saved in Word and PDF. Third, send each one by its method. Fourth, annotate each send with party, method and date, and save the sent letter. Fifth, follow up on receipt. Sixth, switch the status to Dropped and keep the proof. The lazy version flips the status to Dropped and moves on. The high-value version can prove every step. War story: a Case Manager I trained got a call two years after a drop from a client swearing nobody ever told him. She pulled up the note, the logged text, and the signed green Certified Mail card. The call ended in about ninety seconds. An unresponsive client only gets here through the No Contact Protocol, our step-by-step plan for a silent client, and this is where it ends.
rules.ask: {name}, the status says Pending Drop but there's no note. What do you do, and who do you tell?

model.say: Here's the whole close-out on one rail. Before I walk it, {name}, guess which step gets skipped most in a busy week. Hold that thought. Step one, the gate, with its two ticks: Pending Drop, and the client told. Step two, the three letters, client, carrier and provider, each saved in Word and PDF. Step three, the send: the client by her preferred method plus Certified Mail, carriers and providers by email or fax as the CRM says. Step four, annotate and save. Step five, follow up on the return receipt, the acknowledgement and the fax confirmation. Step six, the status flips from Pending Drop to Dropped, proof kept. Closing a file is a lot like spring cleaning. The lazy version shoves everything in the closet and shuts the door. The high-value version labels every box, so when someone opens that closet in two years, it all makes sense. And the step that gets skipped most? Step five, the follow-up.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the follow-up on receipt is the step people skip?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. The trigger is the status Pending Drop, with Atty. Thorne's note that the client was told. You open the CMS, under Documents, where the firm's letter templates live, and prepare each party's Withdrawal Letter from the template, for his signature, and you save each one in Word and PDF. Once the letters are signed, you send each by its method, email, text, fax or Certified Mail, and you log the party, the method and the date in the Communications Log. When the receipts are followed up, you switch the status to Dropped and file the proof in Documents: the receipts, the logs and the attorney's note. Why does all that matter? Because a dropped file can still come back years later as a complaint, and the only thing standing between the firm and trouble is that proof. Every file ends up as the last box in storage someday. Make sure yours is the box nobody has to worry about. {name}, you're up.
job.ask: {name}, where in the CMS would you look first to prove a client was told about the drop?

dodont.say: 3 Clues, 1 Rule, Dropped Case edition. I'll read three clues from a dropped practice file, one at a time. Call it, Do or Don't, and name the rule. {name}, you're on the buzzer, and {name}, you're keeping score. You'll want everything from this lesson: checking the gate before you open the template, sending the client's letter two ways with one of them giving us proof, keeping the reason out of a carrier's or provider's letter, holding the status change until every letter is out and logged, and never telling a client the case is worthless. That last one isn't a style point. Whether a claim had value is Atty. Thorne's to discuss, never ours. Now your mystery for the activity. You're about to meet Denise Harlow. Her file has one detail that decides exactly how her letter has to go out, and another that explains why she's being dropped. Find both before you write a word.
dodont.ask: {name}, if a clue has the client asking what her claim was worth, whose conversation is that, and what do you say?

case.say: This one's a practice matter, not John Doe's file, so don't open it or create it in the CMS. It's 12/09/2026. Meet Denise Harlow. She was rear-ended at a red light on 09/19/2026. Granite Shield Insurance has the BI claim, GS-26-48213, and the CRM, our contact records, says its adjuster, Paul Ostrander, takes email only. She treated at Brookside Physical Therapy from 09/24 to 10/29/2026, then stopped. Now, before I tell you why, {name}, guess why Atty. Thorne is dropping this case. Here's the reveal: she has no Health Plan to pay for care, and Brookside declined a Letter of Protection, which is the firm's written promise to pay the provider out of any settlement. So the status is Pending Drop, and his note from 12/08/2026 says he called Denise, she understood, her address at 87 Alder Creek Dr is confirmed, and she prefers text and email. She got the news by phone first, the way it should be.
case.ask: {name}, before you draft a word, which two things on this file do you check, and where do you find them?

task.say: You'll work in the CMS, under Documents, with the firm's approved letter templates, so you never start from a blank page. Record the gate you checked. Then draft three Withdrawal Letters for Atty. Thorne's signature. Denise's carries the date, her name, the date of loss, the reason in his note's words, and the next step he approves: speak to another attorney promptly, because time limits apply. Granite Shield's and Brookside's carry the date, the client, the date of loss and the claim number, and say only that the firm no longer represents her. Name each send method and why. Then write the close-out log: Word and PDF saved, each send annotated, the follow-up, the switch to Dropped and the proof kept. {name}, you're drafting Denise's letter. {name}, you're on Granite Shield's. And be ready for Denise's call, because she'll ask whether her case was worthless. A tip from experience: the carrier letter is the shortest letter you'll ever write. If yours runs past one paragraph, you've said too much.
task.ask: {name}, what will you say when Denise asks whether her case was worthless, and what will you do next?

check.say: Check your work before you log it. {name}, the gate is recorded: Pending Drop and Atty. Thorne's 12/08/2026 note, both confirmed before anything was prepared. Denise's letter is dated 12/09/2026, names the 09/19/2026 date of loss, quotes his reason and gives the approved next step. Granite Shield's letter shows claim GS-26-48213 and the date of loss, Brookside's asks them to update their records, and neither says why. Every letter is saved in Word and PDF. Denise gets text, email and Certified Mail to 87 Alder Creek Dr, Granite Shield gets email, and Brookside gets a fax. Each send is logged, the follow-up is on 12/16/2026, and the status moves to Dropped only after that, with the proof kept. The lazy close-out sends the letters. The high-value close-out can prove they arrived. I once found a file marked Dropped where the only proof was a sticky note that said sent, probably. Now your mystery: what if 12/16/2026 comes and the receipt isn't back?
check.ask: {name}, does any letter except Denise's mention treatment or insurance, and if it does, what do you fix?

questions.say: Last game of the course: Prove It. I ask, you answer, and every answer needs a name, a date or a method from the file, or it doesn't count. Three questions, answered from the practice matter in your own words, under each one. First, name the two things you confirm before any Withdrawal Letter goes out, and why both matter. Second, tell me what goes in Denise Harlow's letter that doesn't go in Granite Shield's or Brookside's, and why we keep it that way. Third, Denise's letters went out on 12/09/2026: what has to be true before her status becomes Dropped, and what proof stays in the file? {name}, you're first on question one. {name}, you've got question two. Names, dates and methods, please, not general rules.
questions.ask: {name}, which of the three letters is the only one that explains why?

summary.say: Now your self-summary. In your own words, what did you learn closing a Dropped Case? I want the principles behind the close-out, not the clicks. Then your strategy: Denise's letters are out, and on 12/16/2026 her return receipt still hasn't come back. What's your next action, and why is it the right one rather than something else? Be honest about the one thing in this module you're least sure of. Keep the line in mind as you write: if your answer explains the drop to Denise, or tells her what to do next beyond what Atty. Thorne approved, it has crossed into his territory. And remember, the polite breakup letter only works if it actually arrives. {name}, read me your next action out loud when you're done.
summary.ask: {name}, whose job is it to tell Denise why her case was dropped, and what's yours?

scale.say: And here we are, the very last rating of the course. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each skill: confirming the Pending Drop gate before anything goes out, drafting a Withdrawal Letter for each party, choosing and logging each send method, and closing the file with proof and without advice. Submit it, and I'll compare your rating with your answers; a wide gap is a conversation, not a grade. Think back to Day 1. I told you John Doe's file had a detail that could cost him money, and it turned out to be where he was sitting in the car. That's the job. So here's your final challenge, for your very first real file: within the first hour, find one detail nobody has flagged yet, the one that could cost that client money. Write it down, back it with a document, and bring it to your attorney the same day. Do that every time, and someday your files will be the last boxes in storage that nobody ever has to open. {name}, you're up first.
scale.ask: {name}, what's the first thing you'll check on your first real file, and why that one?

why.say: Let's play Guess the Net. Same $40,000.00 gross on both tracks. On Track A, where Keystone settled, John Doe netted $20,359.92. On Track B, Keystone stonewalled, so we sued, mediated and arbitrated, and Laura Whitcomb's award came in on 07/06/2027. Thumbs up if you think John nets more on Track B, thumbs down if less. {name}, you're thumbs down? Give me a number. Here's the reveal: $14,713.75. Same gross, almost six thousand dollars less in his pocket. Three things moved that number, and I'll reveal them one at a time. And yes, when that award check lands, someone in this office will want a photo holding it like a lottery winner. Take the photo. Then it goes straight into trust, because John is going to notice the difference, and he deserves to understand every dollar of it before he signs anything. That's what the Net Sheet is for.
why.ask: {name}, same $40,000.00 gross on both tracks: what's your guess for the three things that pulled John's net down?

theory.say: Plain words first. The Net Sheet is the page that shows the client where every dollar came from and where every dollar goes. Four ideas sit under it. One, the common fund doctrine. That just means everyone who gets paid out of the pot helps pay for the work that filled the pot, so a lienholder, the company that paid a Medical Bill and wants paying back, shares in our fees and costs. That's how we get reductions. Two, the double-dipping trap: counting the same dollar twice, or paying the same bill twice. Carriers audit, so every dollar traces back to its source. Three, fee transparency: each stream of money carries its own fee, tracked separately. Four, the Final Payoff Letter, a signed letter that says this amount settles the bill in full. No letter, no check. {name}, which of those four would you bet a brand-new Case Manager forgets first?
theory.ask: {name}, why should Peach State share in the cost of a lawsuit it never filed?

frame.say: Here's the Master Financial Ledger, top to bottom, and I'll tell you which section is the booby trap at the end. First, the recovery summary: the gross by stream, each with its source, so Keystone's BI tendered at mediation and both UM awards from arbitration. Next, attorney fees, the fee on each stream, confirmed from the retainer, and on this file that's the 40% tier because suit was filed. The fee tier is the percentage in the retainer: a third if the case settles before suit, 40% once suit is filed, because a lawsuit is a lot more work. Then case expenses, every cost the firm advanced, each with its receipt: filing, service, mediation, arbitration, the court reporter, records, plus the pre-suit costs. Then the provider ledger: charges, payments, adjustments, balance owed and reduction, listing only the liens actually owed. Last, the net to the client, line by line. The lazy ledger has the right total. The high-value ledger has the right total and a source for every line. And the booby trap? The provider ledger, where a zero-balance line loves to sneak onto the payables. {name}, keep your eyes on that one.
frame.ask: {name}, which section of this ledger would you check twice on a litigated file, and why?

rules.say: The award ends the case, not the work. Laura Whitcomb's 07/06/2027 award gives Harbor Point's $20,000.00 and Cardinal State's $10,000.00, and with Keystone's $10,000.00 BI from the 03/18/2027 mediation, the gross is $40,000.00. The fee follows the retainer: suit filed 09/24/2026, so 40%, $16,000.00, confirmed by Atty. Thorne. Litigation costs need receipts: filing $218.00, service $285.00, mediation $1,200.00, arbitration $900.00, reporter $645.50, records $160.00, plus the pre-suit $486.75, totaling $3,895.25. The fund pays only what's owed. Peach State's reduction follows the fee charged, $744.00, accepted at $1,116.00, and Riverton Spine & Rehab accepts $4,275.00. Net: $14,713.75. Nothing leaves trust until the checks clear, the Payoff Letters are in and John signs. {name}, the lazy move is copying Track A's numbers. The high-value move is rebuilding every line from this file. You explain the arithmetic; whether suing was worth it is Atty. Thorne's conversation.
rules.ask: {name}, Peach State's reduction was $620.00 on Track A. Why is it $744.00 now?

model.say: Here's the reveal of those three things I promised. Two ledger cards side by side, Track A and Track B, five rows each: gross, fee, costs, liens and net. Both gross rows read $40,000.00. On Track B, three rows light up, the fee, the costs and the liens, because those are the three the lawsuit moved. The fee jumped to the 40% tier, the costs grew with every filing and hearing, and the liens moved because reductions follow the fee actually charged. At the bottom, the nets: $20,359.92 on Track A, $14,713.75 on Track B. Between the cards, the reason: suit filed 09/24/2026. And at the foot, a red reminder for the activity: no Payoff Letter, no payment. {name}, you guessed earlier. How many of the three did you get? Be honest, there's no cake riding on it.
model.ask: {name}, looking at the Track B card, which highlighted row moved the most, and by how much?

job.say: Here's how the close-out runs on the job. The award arrives on 07/06/2027. You log it under Litigation and diary each carrier's payment: Harbor Point $20,000.00 and Cardinal State $10,000.00. Once the fund is known, you prepare the Reduction Requests, our letters asking each lienholder to take less, with the math and the reason, in the LSH Net Sheet and send them for Atty. Thorne's approval, and they come back as Peach State at $1,116.00 and Riverton Spine & Rehab at $4,275.00. When the last UM check has cleared, you complete the Net Sheet and route the Settlement Statement through Tasks, Escalate, the CMS route that drops it in Atty. Thorne's queue with a time stamp, showing a net of $14,713.75, all before John signs anything. War story: I once saw an office order a sheet cake that said WE WON before the second check cleared. The check came back with the payee name wrong, the cake got eaten anyway, and the client waited three more weeks for his money. Celebrate when the money is cleared, not when the envelope arrives. {name}, who decides when the cake gets ordered?
job.ask: {name}, what's the one thing that has to be true before you send John's Settlement Statement to Atty. Thorne?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule, litigated close-out edition. Three clues, one at a time. Call it, Do or Don't, and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, you're keeping score, and {name}, you're on the first buzz. You'll need everything from this lesson: showing John the fee tier from his own retainer, a receipt on every litigation cost, reducing liens at the fee actually charged, and the traps of carrying Track A's numbers into this file, or disbursing Keystone's check, held in trust since 03/29/2027, too early. If any clue tempts you toward an opinion on whether the lawsuit was worth it, stop right there. That's Atty. Thorne's conversation with John. And now a mystery for the next lesson: not every file ends with a check and a cake. Some end with a letter. Who has to hear the news first, and how do we prove they heard it?
dodont.ask: {name}, if a clue mentions 33⅓%, what should that make you suspicious of?

case.say: It's 07/22/2027, and something just landed. Before I tell you what, {name}, guess: good news or bad news? Good news. Laura Whitcomb's 07/06/2027 award gave Harbor Point's $20,000.00 and Cardinal State's $10,000.00. Harbor Point's check came 07/20, and Cardinal State's arrived this morning, joining Keystone's $10,000.00, held in trust since 03/29/2027. That's all $40,000.00 in trust. Peach State accepted $1,116.00 on 07/14, and Riverton Spine & Rehab accepted $4,275.00 on 07/16, both in writing, and every litigation cost has a receipt. Atty. Thorne's note reminds us suit was filed, so the fee is the 40% tier under John's retainer, the agreement he signed with the firm on day one: a third before suit, 40% after. He wants the Net Sheet and the Settlement Statement for his review before John sees anything. And no, nobody orders the cake yet. Open the Net Sheet beside this slide and set it to the Track B stage.
case.ask: {name}, before you enter a single number, what fee percentage applies at the Track B stage, and where does it come from?

task.say: Here's your job. You'll complete John Doe's LSH Net Sheet for the litigated recovery. Section one is the gross by carrier. Section two is the 40% fee and every receipted cost, pre-suit and litigation, each on its own row. Section three lists every provider and payer with charges, payments, adjustments and balance owed, and each lien's reduced figure with its Payoff Letter. Section four is the net to John. Tie it to the Trust Ledger in CMS, which is the record of every dollar sitting in the firm's trust account, then route the Settlement Statement to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate, so it lands in his queue with a record of when it went. {name}, you'll also take John's call. Walk him through fee, costs, liens and net, show the 40% from his own retainer, and give the reduced liens with their acceptances. Clients always have a friend who kept more. Every single one. Your answer is the arithmetic, never an opinion. Hand in a Net Sheet reaching $14,713.75, every number proved.
task.ask: {name}, John says a friend kept way more from his settlement. What do you say, word for word?

check.say: Check your Net Sheet before you log it, and I'm calling on people. {name}, the gross: Keystone $10,000.00 from mediation, plus Harbor Point $20,000.00 and Cardinal State $10,000.00 from the award, $40,000.00. The fee is the 40% tier, $16,000.00, confirmed from the retainer, not 33⅓% out of habit. Costs come to $3,895.25, each on its row with a receipt. Liens: Peach State from $1,860.00 down to $1,116.00, and Riverton Spine & Rehab from $6,290.00 to the audited $6,105.00 to $4,275.00, totaling $5,391.00. Zero-balance lines like PIP's $5,000.00 and Crescent's $1,540.00 write-off stay off the payables. Net $14,713.75, tied to the $40,000.00 in trust. Nothing disbursed until John signs on 07/29/2027, disbursement 07/30/2027. And no lien paid from a phone call. The lazy sheet matches the total. The high-value sheet survives an audit. Now your mystery: one number on somebody's sheet in this room snuck in from Track A. Whose, and which one?
check.ask: {name}, does your Trust Ledger tie to the $40,000.00 gross to the cent, and if not, where's the gap?

questions.say: Final round of the game show, and the jackpot question is the whole case. John Doe's file is now closed, from intake all the way to the award, so take a second to appreciate that. You carried one file through every phase. Answer from the file, in your own words, typed under each question. Take the $40,000.00 award down to John's $14,713.75, naming every deduction with its figure and source. Explain why the fee is 40% on this file, which document says so and who confirms it. And show why Peach State accepted $1,240.00 on Track A but $1,116.00 on Track B. {name}, you're my lightning-round contestant: I'll ask you one of these out loud when time's up. And {name}, you're the judge. If you hear a number without a source, you buzz.
questions.ask: {name}, quick-fire: which document tells us the fee on this file is 40%?

summary.say: Now your self-summary, in your own words. Keep Question 5 in mind as you write, because it's the UPL gate, which is the line between explaining facts and giving legal advice: arithmetic, yes; opinion, no. If you write that the lawsuit was or wasn't worth it, you've crossed the line, however good the rest is. Then your scenario: it's 01/28/2027, John's been unreachable for six days, his deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027, and defense counsel wants to inspect Margaret's Civic. Give me your next five actions, in order, and who owns each one. Here's why I bring back an old moment. The best Case Managers I've worked with can tell you a file's whole story from memory, like a favorite movie. The ones who struggle remember only the last scene. {name}, which kind are you going to be?
summary.ask: {name}, where exactly is the line between explaining John's net and judging whether suing was worth it?

scale.say: Here's your Skill Scale for the award and the Net Sheet. Score yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, then submit it for review. I'll sit down with your rating beside your score, and if there's a wide gap either way, we'll talk it through together. Be as honest about yourself as you've been with John's numbers. {name}, no all-fives just because the case is won; the award check doesn't grade your work, the Net Sheet does. And keep your pen out, because we've got one more file to close, and it's not a winner. Denise Harlow's case is dropped. Here's the mystery to carry into that check: when a case ends without a check, what's left in the file that proves the firm did its job?
scale.ask: {name}, looking back across John Doe's whole file, which skill do you feel strongest in now?

why.say: Quick game: Who Has to Answer? I'll name someone, you shout “has to” or “doesn't have to” answer our questions right now. Robert Smith, the defendant. The hospital's records custodian. Ruth Calloway, the witness. {name}, you take the tiebreaker on Ruth. Here's the reveal: Robert Smith has to, because he's a party in the lawsuit. The custodian and Ruth Calloway don't, not unless the court commands it. That command is a subpoena. It's powerful, and it comes with rules. Serve it out of order, write it too broadly, or let the records come back after discovery closes on 05/28/2027, and Atty. Thorne could walk into trial without the evidence. And trust me, the first time you call a records department, someone will cheerfully tell you they've “never heard of” a patient whose MRI they did. Today you learn to make that phone call go very differently.
why.ask: {name}, who on John Doe's file holds evidence we need but owes us nothing unless the court commands it?

theory.say: Two tools, two different jobs. A Subpoena Duces Tecum, which is Latin for “bring it with you,” orders someone outside the lawsuit to produce documents, like a hospital, a phone company or an employer. A trial subpoena orders a witness to show up and testify: fact witnesses, treating doctors, police officers. Now the warning. A request for “all records of any kind” is what the other side calls a fishing expedition, and they can file a Motion to Quash, which asks the court to cancel it. The model is narrow: emergency room records, triage notes and imaging, one client, the accident date only. The lazy subpoena asks for everything and gets nothing. The high-value one asks for exactly what we need and gets it fast. And the order never changes: you draft, you notice opposing counsel, you serve the custodian, and you track compliance. {name}, remember this: notice comes first.
theory.ask: {name}, why would a court care whether a subpoena is narrow, even when the records are about our own client?

rules.say: Here's how it runs on John Doe's file. The trigger is a refused request, or a record Atty. Thorne needs from its custodian. You ask him whether he wants a records subpoena, and he decides, signs and issues it. You draft on the court-approved form with the case style, Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417, the named custodian and a narrow Exhibit A: one subject, exact dates, named record types. A copy goes to Atty. Grant Mercer first, and only after the notice period does Allied Process Services serve the custodian. Five days before production you make the compliance call, and you pay the copy invoice promptly, because an unpaid invoice is the most popular reason records go missing. Everything comes back before 05/28/2027. Trial subpoenas go only to the witnesses Atty. Thorne names, tasked against 08/12/2027 and 09/13/2027. {name}, why do you think we call five days before, not the day of?
rules.ask: {name}, if the custodian tells you on the compliance call that the request is too broad, what do you do?

job.say: Let's run one through. Atty. Thorne needs the Riverton Fire Run Report from its custodian. You route that question to him through Tasks, and you draft nothing until he decides. Once he approves, you build it from the template with a narrow Exhibit A: run RF-26-0206-114, Medic 7, John Doe, 02/06/2026 only. The notice to Atty. Mercer is dated before service, every single time. I once audited a file where the notice and the service had the same date, and the defense argued for a month about which happened first. Nobody wins that argument. Then, while it's open, you review its row in the subpoena log every ten days, call the custodian five days before production, and log each reading with its date. Any miss goes to Atty. Thorne. Why? Because a record that arrives after discovery closes may never reach the jury. So here's your mystery, {name}: which record on John Doe's file is most likely to need a subpoena next?
job.ask: {name}, which two dates on a subpoena log row tell you, at a glance, whether notice came first?

case.say: Show of hands: who's ever sent an important email and then found the reply sitting in spam three days later? Keep them up. {name}, that's a lot of hands, and that's exactly why we check. It's the twenty-second of September twenty twenty-six, and we're on Track B, the litigation track, the road where the case goes to court. The file went to Litigation on the tenth, on Atty. Thorne's authorization, and the filing target is the twenty-fourth, so today is our forty-eight-hour audit, our two-day check that everything's ready before we file. This morning he approved his Complaint against Robert Smith in the State Court of Riverton County. The Complaint is the document that starts the lawsuit. What we don't have yet is the civil cover sheet and the summons, the court's notice telling Robert Smith he's being sued. And there's a trap in the CMS: an older draft from the fifteenth, stamped not for filing, unsigned, no case number. Once the envelope is accepted, the fee tier moves to forty percent and the court's clocks start. Two Complaints, one court. Only one of them should ever leave this building.
case.ask: {name}, two Complaints sit in the CMS today. How will you make sure the right one reaches the court?

task.say: Four moves. First, tag Nadia Brooks on the Litigation Desk with a task she can act on without calling you: the cover sheet and the summons, built from the Complaint he approved this morning, due tonight, routed to Atty. Thorne for signature. He signs on the twenty-third. Second, on the twenty-fourth, you build the envelope in Court E-Filing, the court's online filing system: the caption, the court, the three documents, the filing attorney and the two hundred eighteen dollar fee, and you open every page to check his signature first. Third, when it's accepted, you record the case number, file the stamped Complaint, the summons and the conference notice, and post the fee. And yes, check your spam folder for the acceptance email, because court systems love sending the most important message of the month straight to junk. Fourth, you calendar what the filing starts, and you hold what it doesn't. {name}, you're Nadia; {name}, you're writing her the task. Make it so clear she never has to call you.
task.ask: {name}, which deadline can you calendar the day you file, and which one has to wait? Why?

check.say: Check your work against this, and {name}, you're grading the person next to you. Your task to Nadia names the documents, the approved Complaint, the due date and Atty. Thorne as signer. Nothing went in unsigned, and the September fifteenth draft never left the CMS. The envelope was accepted on the twenty-fourth as twenty-six CV zero four four one seven, and that number replaced Pending in the court fields. Three named PDFs sit in zero one pleadings, and costs read seven hundred four dollars seventy-five. The service deadline, the last day to formally deliver the lawsuit to Robert Smith, is January twenty-second, twenty twenty-seven, a Friday, a hundred and twenty days out, with alerts. Allied Process Services has its hand-off. The conference is December tenth at nine, with Atty. Thorne attending. And the answer date says set on service. The lazy file has a case number. The excellent one has every clock that number started. Your mystery for the next block: Allied hasn't served him yet. What happens to our calendar if they can't find Robert Smith?
check.ask: {name}, if the answer date had been calendared today, what would it have been counted from, and why is that wrong?
